newsitem.title: GERMANY: Russia ambassador says room for seized art talks.
newsitem.headline: Russia ambassador says room for seized art talks.

text.p: Russia's ambassador in Bonn, Vladislav Terekhov, said on Thursday there was still room for talks on the ownership of works of art seized by the Red Army from Nazi Germany during World War Two.
The Russian parliament approved a draft law on Wednesday handing ownership of the art, including treasures from ancient Troy and priceless paintings by Henri Matisse, over to Russia.
Both the Russian and German governments have criticised it and Terekhov told Germany's Saar Radio in an interview that they were negotiating to seek a compromise.
"I would advise against stoking up the atmosphere," Terekhov said, adding he was sure the deadlock could be broken in a reasonable way.

Terekhov said it was conceivable President Boris Yeltsin would refuse to sign the draft law and would hand it back to parliament for revision. Russian deputy culture minister Mikhail Shvydkoi has urged Yeltsin not to sign it.
Germany has demanded the return of the artefacts seized by Soviet soldiers at the end of World War Two from museums and private homes in Germany, and has appealed to Yeltsin for help several times.
But many Russians view the treasures as compensation for Russian works of art destroyed by the Nazis and the wartime losses of the Soviet Union.

Terekhov said the former Soviet Union had already given back 90 percent of the art seized during the war, whereas very few of the "countless cultural treasures" lost during the Nazi occupation had been returned.

One German expert close to the talks has indicated Germany might be ready to leave some artefacts in Russia and become involved in a series of Russian cultural projects as a show of political goodwill.
